https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-minis.text: BRUSSELS — After days of recriminations over the sudden arrival of tens of thousands of migrants in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta last week, the EU’s 27 home affairs ministers are expected to use an emergency meeting Tuesday to express solidarity with Madrid and focus on how to prevent a repeat. However, Spain will also criticize some governments for turning the crisis into an attack on Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez instead of supporting a fellow EU country facing an emergency, according to an official familiar with Madrid’s plans, granted anonymity to speak freely. Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska will present Madrid’s assessment of the events and make the case for a common European response, the official said. After initial criticism of Spain, the mood among EU capitals has softened as the immediate crisis eased, according to eight diplomats from different countries who were granted anonymity to speak freely. Almost all the migrants who entered the exclave last week have returned to Morocco, Spanish authorities say, and there has been no reported onward movement into mainland Europe. Advertisement Advertisement The groundwork for Tuesday’s meeting was set on Monday when EU ambassadors held talks that lasted around two and a half hours. The Spanish envoy gave Madrid’s account of the Ceuta crisis, during which more than 70 people died, and reprimanded some capitals for spreading disinformation, according to one of the diplomats. The ambassador was asked for verification of Madrid’s figures on returned migrants and for the situation to be closely monitored, two other diplomats said. Concerns were also raised that Spanish government policies may have been used by people-smugglers and gangs to encourage the events in Ceuta. “There’s a concern that … the legalization of a million irregular migrants, that it’s been possible [for people-smugglers] to use that to give the impression that the door was open,” said one diplomat from a country that has been critical of Spain. Italy called for the EU to immediately establish migrant deportation hubs in non-EU countries, one of the diplomats said. The plans follow the approval of a law granting EU capitals the power to set up centers in non-EU countries for processing migrants who have been denied the right to stay in the bloc — so-called return hubs. But the Spanish ambassador criticized Italy for amplifying false claims about the migrant regularization program, such as Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani’s suggestion on social media that it automatically grants EU citizenship. The program provides legal residency to eligible migrants but does not confer Spanish nationality. Rallying to support Spain Commission President Ursula von der Leyen set the tone of conciliation on Monday by writing to Sánchez to praise Spain and Morocco for their handling of the crisis and calling for a united European response. She said the episode showed the need for stronger controls at the EU’s external borders, closer cooperation with partner countries, better early-warning systems, action against smuggling networks and more effective returns. Advertisement Advertisement The interior ministers are expected to seek further rapprochement. Tuesday’s discussion will focus on lessons learned from Ceuta, ways to beef up controls at the bloc’s external borders and how to respond to potential future episodes of instrumentalized migration, rather than assigning blame for the crisis, three of the diplomats said. “Everyone is both very willing and very eager to help, and acknowledged this has been a very difficult situation for Spain,” one of the EU diplomats said after the ambassadors’ gathering. The diplomat said Monday’s meeting had been calmer than the weekend’s public exchanges. Twenty-two national leaders, in a letter initiated by Italy and Denmark, had on Saturday called for tougher external borders and warned against policies that could act as “pull factors” — an apparent reference to Spain’s plan to grant legal status to more than 1 million undocumented migrants . Madrid saw the letter as an attempt to blame the Spanish government for a crisis not of its making. Tuesday’s videoconference will be chaired by Ireland’s Justice Minister Jim O’Callaghan. Officials from EU border agency Frontex, the EU Asylum Agency, Europol, the European External Action Service and Schengen-associated countries will also participate. The crisis has already pushed migration higher up the EU agenda. The issue was already meant to feature at the October European Council summit, but officials now expect it to play a much more prominent role in the run-up to that meeting, the diplomats said. The Commission is expected to consider possible new migration measures in September, after examining what caused the sudden influx and whether social media or other actors helped organize or amplify it, three of the diplomats said. Strengthening Frontex is one option, with the Commission indicating to ambassadors Monday that it could propose additional steps to reinforce the agency’s role, according to the diplomats. Max Griera contributed reporting. This article has been updated. Advertisement Advertisement

https://baltic-review.com/tallinn-food-t.text: Share Tweet 0 Tallinn’s Telliskivi Creative City is hosting the Food Truck Festival on 8–9 August 2026. A food festival in a neighbourhood shaped by reuse Visitors to Tallinn’s Telliskivi Creative City are being offered a distinctly urban weekend experience as the Tallinn Food Truck Festival takes place on Saturday and Sunday, 8–9 August 2026. The event brings more than 50 food trucks to the former industrial quarter, alongside a concert programme, DJ sets and public voting for the festival’s best food truck. The festival is a current, small-scale example of how Tallinn’s former industrial spaces continue to function as public places rather than simply as preserved buildings. Telliskivi’s courtyards and former factory structures are being used for food, culture, commerce and social activity, giving the northern Tallinn district a temporary pedestrian focus during the height of the summer season. From railway workshops to a creative district Telliskivi Creative City is located in a former industrial complex between the Kalamaja and Pelgulinn areas. According to Visit Tallinn, the old factory buildings have been adapted for galleries, studios, cafés, restaurants and cultural venues. The city tourism office describes the site as a cultural and business centre where industrial heritage and contemporary creativity meet. The transformation is part of a wider change in northern Tallinn. Places that were once associated mainly with manufacturing, storage and railway activity have gradually become accessible urban destinations. Their value now lies not only in the buildings themselves, but also in the way they connect different uses: workspaces, independent shops, restaurants, exhibitions and public events. Telliskivi’s own history records the start of its redevelopment in the late 2000s. The creative district now presents itself as a community platform for Estonia’s creative industries, with events and businesses operating alongside the retained industrial character of the site. That combination gives the food festival a setting that is more distinctive than a conventional temporary market on an open square. A temporary route through the city The 2026 festival is organised as an open-air event at Telliskivi 60. The official event listing says that participating vendors include Estonian food businesses and street-food operators from neighbouring countries. The programme also includes a burger-eating competition on both days, while visitors can vote on awards in two categories: Best Design and Best Food. Those details make the festival more than a collection of stalls. The event creates a temporary route through the creative city, encouraging visitors to move between food points, music and the surrounding businesses. In a district already known for galleries, restaurants and design, the festival adds another layer of activity without requiring a new permanent structure. Such events also show how urban districts can accommodate different rhythms. During ordinary weekdays, Telliskivi functions as a mixed business and cultural quarter. At weekends, its courtyards can support markets, performances and social gatherings. The food-truck format is particularly suited to that flexibility because it can occupy existing public space for a limited period and then leave the area available for its regular uses. Public space, local business and visitor flow For Tallinn, the festival contributes to the city’s broader visitor offer while remaining rooted in a neighbourhood rather than a single landmark. Telliskivi is close to Balti Jaam railway station and within walking distance of the Old Town, making it part of a wider movement corridor between the historic centre, the railway area and northern districts. The event listing does not make claims about visitor numbers or economic impact, so its significance should not be overstated. Its immediate contribution is more straightforward: it gives food entrepreneurs a shared platform, offers residents and visitors a reason to spend time in the district, and demonstrates how adapted industrial environments can host public life. That is also why Telliskivi remains relevant to discussions about urban development. The area illustrates a model in which regeneration is not limited to new construction. Existing structures, open courtyards and a recognisable local identity can support new activity while preserving traces of the city’s industrial past. A summer event with an urban backdrop The Tallinn Food Truck Festival continues through Sunday, 9 August. Its combination of food, music and audience voting is deliberately accessible, but the setting gives the weekend a larger urban dimension. Visitors are not only attending a festival; they are experiencing a district whose current identity has been built by layering new uses onto an older industrial landscape. For Tallinn, that is a constructive story about city life: a former closed production area now functioning as an open meeting place, with short-term events helping to keep the public realm active and commercially diverse. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A higher paycheck makes healthier eating easier, according to a new CDC report. Photograph: StockSeller_ukr/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A higher paycheck makes healthier eating easier, according to a new CDC report. Photograph: StockSeller_ukr/Getty Images Trump administration Likelihood of eating fresh produce increases with income for US adults, new CDC report shows The report highlights deep divides between low- and middle- income, a disparity that dates back decades Jessica Glenza Sat 19 Sep 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 09.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reaffirms that adults are more likely to eat fresh fruits and vegetables as their income increases. The data brief comes as Republican cuts to food assistance programs, colloquially called “food stamps”, have led enrollment to “ plummet ”. Changes to US dietary guidelines, led by health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr , have also made a government-recommended diet more expensive. A new “food pyramid” released in January emphasized animal protein, fresh fruit and vegetables, all of which cost more, according to studies. Some experts say the new US dietary guidelines have ‘conflicting messaging’. Here’s who will be affected most Read more “Particularly for people with lower incomes this is really infeasible, especially when millions of people – and what will be probably millions of children – are going to lose access to a really critical benefit that keeps people food secure,” said Priya Fielding-Singh, director of policy and programs at the George Washington University Global Food Institute. The data brief from CDC’s National Center for Health Statistics found that more than nine in 10 Americans ate any vegetable on a given day and about 7 in 10 ate any fruit. The data brief covered adults older than 20 from August 2021-2023. However, the percentage of adults who ate any vegetables, “dark green vegetables, red or orange vegetables, and other vegetable types increased with increasing family income” – with deep divides between the low-income and middle class. For instance, the percentage of adults who ate any fruit on a given day was 56% for people living on less than 130% of the federal poverty level ($20,748 for a single adult). By contrast, 76% of people who earned 350% of FPL ($55,860) ate any fruit. Similarly, a single person who earned $55,860 was almost twice as likely (38% versus 19.6%) to eat berries, citrus and melons compared to the poorest people included in the study. The same was true of vegetables. Although most Americans ate a vegetable in a day, only 29% of the lowest income Americans in the data brief ate a dark green vegetable, compared to 42% for the highest income. This is not surprising. Years of studies have shown that people with less money and time spend more on energy-dense, shelf-stable packaged foods – foods that fill you up and don’t spoil. The relationship between food and income was known even 91 years ago, when a study of diet and income in the UK found that nearly everyone ate potatoes and bread, but the poorest in society bought far less milk, eggs, vegetables and fruits. “A review of the state of health of the people of the different groups suggests that, as income increases, disease and death-rate decrease, children grow more quickly, adult stature is greater and general health and physique improve,” Sir John Boyd Orr wrote in 1935 . Multiple contemporary studies have pointed out the same tension. A recent study by University of Washington researchers found foods recommended by Kennedy’s health department cost a mean of $15.82 per day . The average Snap household is two people and receives $177 per month , or about $3 per day per person. About 39% of Snap beneficiaries are children. Republican cuts to food assistance programs in the “Big Beautiful Bill” act mean that fewer Americans are getting these benefits. Republicans required states to pay toward food benefits for the first time, barred certain legal immigrants (particularly people in the US on asylum and certain trafficking survivors) from food assistance programs, and required older people to submit to work requirements, raising the age for people required to prove they work 20 hours a week from 54 to 64. Republicans also required states to pay a share of food assistance benefits for the first time in the program’s history, which could result in hundreds of millions of dollars of new costs in some states, according to the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities . All of this is contributing to a swift decline in food assistance rates. Food assistance enrollment fell 13% nationally between May 2025 and May 2026 , according to an Associated Press analysis. In some states the declines have been even more dramatic, such as Florida, Georgia, Louisiana and Nevada. In these states, proponents of welfare cuts argue that people are no longer eligible because they’re earning more money. Republicans also imposed new documentation requirements, making it more likely that eligible people will fail to complete paperwork. In Arizona, some analysts said this appears to be contributing to the 47% reduction in enrollees in the state, where new documentation requirements are running headlong into severe staff shortages . Pamela Lachman, chief strategy officer for the Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO), a group that works with people recently released from jail and prison, said that the administrative burdens simply do not consider the reality of daily life for people seeking food assistance. CEO’s own part-time work programs are often difficult to count as work for the purposes of food assistance, because hours can be irregular. “They have requirements to do their parole supervision, they’re trying to find a place to live – all of those things mean your work might be inconsistent,” said Lachman. “If you immediately need to start proving you’re working 20 hours a week, if not more, that’s very challenging to do.” Even as fewer Americans access food benefits, it is likely the government will have less insight into food insecurity. In September 2025 , the US Department of Agriculture announced it would no longer sponsor the Food Security Supplement in the US Census Bureau’s annual survey, ending data collection that had occurred annually since 1995.
